title: Understanding emotion-focused coping: What decades of psychology research reveal
excerpt:
When life brings a stressful demand that feels bigger than what we can easily handle, psychologists call our mental and behavioral efforts to manage that pressure “coping.” Rather than acting as a fixed habit that never changes, coping is an active process that shifts as stressful situations unfold.

In a landmark 1980 study , psychologists Susan Folkman and Richard Lazarus tracked 100 men and women aged 45 to 64 for an entire year, analyzing 1,332 everyday stressful events. They divided coping into two main jobs: problem-focused coping, which tries to alter or fix the stressful situation itself, and emotion-focused coping, which tries to soothe or regulate the painful feelings sparked by the event.

People almost never rely on just one approach at a time, using both problem-focused and emotion-focused coping together in 98 percent of those 1,332 episodes. As Lazarus later warned in a passage highlighted by Jennifer Austenfeld and Annette Stanton’s 2004 review , treating problem-focused and emotion-focused coping as rigid, separate action boxes or pitting one against the other as the winner misses how real coping works…

Healthy adults who take a single dose of the prescription stimulant methylphenidate, commonly sold as Ritalin, tend to cheat less for money than those given an inactive placebo, according to new research published in Psychopharmacology . Comparing methylphenidate against both a placebo and a non-stimulant medication, the researchers found evidence that this drop in dishonesty was not a byproduct of sharper focus, mood shifts, or expectations about the pill.

title: Fermilab-led team builds ultrafast ‘stopwatch’ for particle detectors
excerpt:
Knowing the when and where of subatomic particle interactions inside a detector is essential for physicists to understand exactly what happened, what kind of particles were involved, and to tell one signal from another. Future high-energy physics experiments will require detectors that can track an unprecedented number of signals from particles while distinguishing between signals occurring only trillionths of a second apart. This feat will depend on custom-made, innovative electronics and sensors that quickly and precisely determine when and where particles pass.

To help meet this challenge, a team at the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, led by scientist Artur Apresyan, developed a new, ultrafast readout chip called the Fermilab Constant Fraction Discriminator, or FCFD.

The Fermilab Constant Fraction Discriminator, or FCFD, is a custom, ultrafast readout chip designed at Fermilab, translates signals from passing particles into measurable, analyzable data at unprecedented speeds and accuracy levels. The chip will be crucial for next-generation experiments like those at the Electron-Ion Collider. Credit: Ryan Postel, Fermilab…

excerpt:
A comprehensive review of mental health research published in JAMA Psychiatry indicates that scientists use the terms “neurodiversity” and “neurodivergent” inconsistently, applying them to two dozen distinct clinical categories or leaving out medical criteria altogether. Most of the reviewed studies relied on participants’ self-identification or self-reported diagnoses rather than clinical records, frequently grouping varied conditions such as autism, ADHD, dyslexia, and anxiety under a single umbrella.
